# What GitHub Actions is {#sec-overview .unnumbered}

GitHub Actions runs commands on GitHub's machines when something happens in a
repository: a push, a pull request, a tag, or a time of day. A workflow is a
YAML file in `.github/workflows/` that says on which events it runs and what its
jobs do. Each job runs on a fresh machine, a runner, which has an operating
system and a set of common tools but nothing of the project, not even its code,
until the steps of the job fetch and install it. That is the point of
continuous integration: a job that passes shows that the project installs and
its tests pass from what the repository declares, not from the state of
someone's laptop. Almost everything that surprises newcomers follows from that:
tools that are missing, files that vanish between jobs, variables that vanish
between steps, and a pull request tested as something other than its branch
(@sec-model). Working with GitHub Actions comes down to writing workflow files
and reading the logs of their runs (@sec-usage).

The tests of a package should run automatically on every change, across the
versions it supports ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-testing)), and so
should the test of a workflow on its small dataset
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-end-to-end)) and the build of the
documentation ([](../../principles/documenting.qmd#sec-docs-as-code)). For a
repository on GitHub, GitHub Actions is where that happens, on the commits and
tags of [](git.qmd).

Checked against GitHub Actions in October 2026, with the actions of the
examples at the versions they name.


# How GitHub Actions thinks {#sec-model}

An event starts a workflow, a workflow runs jobs, and a job runs steps:

```default
event      a push, a pull request, a tag, a schedule, a click
  |
workflow   .github/workflows/tests.yml, which runs on the event
  |
jobs       test, Python 3.12      test, Python 3.15      docs
             each on a fresh runner, all at the same time
  |
steps      check out  ->  install  ->  test
             one after the other, on the runner of their job
```


## Events, workflows, jobs, and steps {#sec-terms}

An event, such as a push to a branch, starts every workflow of the repository
that runs on it, and each start is a run: one execution of the workflow, for one
commit. A workflow holds jobs, which run at the same time, each on a runner of
its own, unless a job names others with `needs` and waits for them. A job holds
steps, which run one after the other on its runner and share its files. A step
either runs commands, with `run`, or an action, with `uses`: a step that someone
has published, such as `actions/checkout`, which fetches the code of the
repository, named by its repository and a version, as in `actions/checkout@v7`.
The result of each job is a check, shown next to the commit and in the pull
request, and a job fails when one of its steps does.


## Every job starts from nothing {#sec-fresh}

A runner is a virtual machine made for one job and deleted after it. It starts
with an operating system and the tools of its image, such as Git, compilers,
and several versions of Python, but without the code of the project, its
dependencies, or anything that an earlier job or run left behind. Every job
therefore checks out the code and installs what it needs before it runs
anything, and a job that passes shows that the repository holds everything the
project needs ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-declared-inputs)).

Nothing passes from one job to another, or from one run to the next, unless the
workflow passes it (@sec-passing). An artifact is a set of files that a job
uploads and that later jobs of the run, or people, download, kept for 90 days. A
cache saves files under a key, such as a hash of the lock file, from which later
runs restore them, to install faster. A cache only saves time: it is deleted
after a week without use, and a job must give the same result without it.

The image is an input too. Its tools change from month to month, and a label
such as `ubuntu-latest` moves to the next version of the operating system when
GitHub decides, so a job that relies on what the image happens to hold breaks,
or computes differently, without a change of its own. Name the version of the
image, such as `ubuntu-24.04`, and install the versions of the language and the
tools that the job needs.


## A run tests a commit, and a pull request its merge {#sec-commits}

Each run belongs to one commit, and its checks are attached to it. A run for a
push tests the commit pushed. A run for a pull request does not test the tip of
its branch: it tests a merge commit that GitHub makes of the branch and its
target, so that the checks show whether `main` would pass after the merge. The
checks run again with every push to the branch, but not when `main` moves on:
the checks of a pull request that passed last week describe a merge with last
week's `main`. While a pull request has a merge conflict, no checks run at all.
A ruleset of the repository can require the checks to pass, and the branch to
be up to date with `main`, before a pull request can be merged.


## A matrix makes many jobs of one {#sec-matrix}

`strategy.matrix` turns one job into one per combination of its values, such as
three operating systems and two versions of Python into six jobs (@sec-test).
This is how a package is tested across the versions it supports
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-testing)): the oldest and the newest version
of the language, and of the libraries the newest that the package allows and
the oldest. The oldest versions are installed only by a job that asks for them,
as uv does with `--resolution lowest-direct`; a lower bound that no job installs
is never tested.

By default, a job of the matrix that fails cancels the others, which hides
whether the failure belongs to one combination or to all; `fail-fast: false`
lets every job finish. A matrix makes at most 256 jobs.


## Each step is a new shell {#sec-shell}

Each `run` step is a script of its own, run by a new shell. A directory changed
with `cd`, a variable set with `export`, and an environment activated in one
step are gone in the next; a step passes variables on to the later steps by
appending them to the file `$GITHUB_ENV` (@sec-passing).

Without `shell`, a step runs in `bash -e` on Linux and macOS: it stops at the
first command that fails, but not when a command fails within a pipe, since a
pipe returns the status of its last command. `pytest | tee test.log` then
passes when the tests fail ([](../../principles/testing.qmd#sec-can-fail)).
With `shell: bash`, which `defaults` sets for every step (@sec-test), it runs in
`bash -eo pipefail`, where a pipe fails when any command in it does.

An expression, `${{ … }}`, is replaced in the text of the script before the
shell runs it. A value that someone else controls, such as the title of a pull
request, thereby becomes part of the script, and a title that holds a command
runs it, with the rights of the job (@sec-permissions). Pass such values through
`env`, such as `TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}`, and use them in
the script as variables, `"$TITLE"`.


## A job runs with the rights it is given {#sec-permissions}

Each job receives a token, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, with which its steps act on the
repository, such as to read the code, publish a release, or comment on a pull
request, and which expires when the job ends. `permissions` sets what it may
do, and every permission that is not named is then none: `contents: read` at
the top of a workflow lets its jobs read the code and nothing else, and a job
that publishes asks for more itself. Secrets, such as the token of a package
index, are stored in the settings of the repository and given to a step as
`${{ secrets.NAME }}`. They are masked in the logs, and they are not passed to
runs for a pull request from a fork, whose token can only read. A workflow on
`pull_request_target` runs with the secrets and rights of the repository for a
pull request from anyone: never check out and run its code there.

An action is code that someone else wrote, run with these rights and secrets.
Whoever controls its repository can move a tag such as `@v7` to other code,
which then runs in your next job; a full commit hash cannot be moved. The
actions of GitHub, in `actions/`, run with the trust you already place in
GitHub; name other actions by the hash of a release, with the version in a
comment (@sec-test), and let Dependabot update both (@sec-dependabot). GitHub's
lockfile of actions, `.github/workflows/actions.lock`, written by
`gh actions-lock`, records the commit of every action, including the actions
that actions use themselves, but is still in public preview.


# Working with GitHub Actions {#sec-usage}

The examples test a Python package with uv. The same shape holds for other
languages, with other actions for the setup (@sec-test).


## Test a package on every change {#sec-test}

```yaml
# .github/workflows/tests.yml
name: Tests

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 5 * * 1"  # Mondays at 05:00 UTC
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: tests-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.sha }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 30
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-24.04, macos-26, windows-2025]
        python: ["3.12", "3.15"]
        resolution: [highest]
        include:
          - os: ubuntu-24.04
            python: "3.12"
            resolution: lowest-direct
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      # astral-sh/setup-uv v10.3.0
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@1c37ad07a6a961277cf70c0d37d6f313000f5884
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python }}
      - name: Install
        run: uv sync --upgrade --resolution ${{ matrix.resolution }}
      - name: Test
        run: uv run --no-sync pytest
```

The workflow runs on every push to `main`, on every pull request, by hand, and
every Monday, so that a new release of a dependency that breaks the package
shows up within a week rather than with the next change. The matrix makes seven
jobs: three operating systems with the oldest and the newest Python that the
package supports, each with the newest versions of its dependencies, and one
with the oldest versions that `pyproject.toml` allows (@sec-matrix).
`uv sync --upgrade` installs the newest versions rather than those of the lock
file, which a library leaves to its users
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-pin)), and `--no-sync` keeps `uv run` from
installing again. `timeout-minutes` stops a job that hangs after 30 minutes
instead of six hours, the default. `concurrency` puts the runs of a pull request
into one group, in which a new run cancels the one before it, and gives every
other run a group of its own, the commit, so that each commit of `main` keeps
its result.

A workflow, whose environment is pinned, installs from its lock file instead,
with `uv sync --locked`, which fails if the lock file is out of date, and its
test runs it on its small dataset, such as with `snakemake --profile
profiles/test` ([](../workflows/snakemake.qmd#sec-run)). An R package is checked
with the steps of `r-lib/actions`, which `usethis::use_github_action()` writes
into a workflow:

```yaml
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: ${{ matrix.r }}
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies@v2
        with:
          extra-packages: any::rcmdcheck
          needs: check
      - uses: r-lib/actions/check-r-package@v2
```


## Triggers {#sec-triggers}

```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]    # commits pushed to main
    tags: ["v*"]        # tags such as v1.2.0
  pull_request:         # pull requests, as merged into their target
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 5 * * 1" # Mondays at 05:00 UTC, on the default branch
  workflow_dispatch:    # by hand, on GitHub or with gh workflow run
  release:
    types: [published]  # a release published on GitHub
```

A scheduled run tests the default branch, starts at a time in UTC, often some
minutes late when GitHub is busy, and is turned off in a public repository after
60 days without activity. A tag or a commit that a workflow pushes with its
`GITHUB_TOKEN` starts no workflow, so that workflows cannot start each other
without end; a workflow that releases a version therefore runs on the tag that
a person pushes (@sec-tag-release).


## The keys used most {#sec-keys}

| Key | Says |
|-------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| `on` | The events the workflow runs on (@sec-triggers) |
| `permissions` | What the token of each job may do (@sec-permissions) |
| `concurrency` | Which runs cancel, or wait for, each other |
| `defaults.run.shell` | The shell of every `run` step (@sec-shell) |
| `env` | Variables of the workflow, a job, or a step |
| `jobs.<id>.runs-on` | The image of the runner, such as `ubuntu-24.04` |
| `jobs.<id>.needs` | The jobs that must succeed before this one starts |
| `jobs.<id>.if` | A condition, such as `github.event_name == 'push'` |
| `jobs.<id>.strategy.matrix` | The values that make one job many (@sec-matrix) |
| `jobs.<id>.timeout-minutes` | When the job is stopped; 360 by default |
| `jobs.<id>.outputs` | Values that the jobs that need this one read (@sec-passing) |
| `steps[*].uses`, `with` | An action, and its inputs |
| `steps[*].run` | Commands, run by a new shell |
| `steps[*].id`, `name` | A name for later steps, and a title for the log |
| `steps[*].if` | A condition, such as `failure()`, true after a failed step |


## Pass files and values on {#sec-passing}

```yaml
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0     # all commits and tags, for git describe
      - id: version
        run: echo "name=$(git describe --tags --always)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - run: echo "MPLBACKEND=Agg" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"  # for every later step
      - run: uv run --no-sync pytest --basetemp=test-output
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        if: failure()        # only after a step has failed
        with:
          name: test-output-${{ steps.version.outputs.name }}-${{ matrix.os }}
          path: test-output/
```

A step writes its outputs to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`, and later steps read them as
`steps.<id>.outputs`; a job passes them on through `outputs`, and the jobs that
need it read them as `needs.<job>.outputs`. `$GITHUB_ENV` sets variables for
every later step of the job. An artifact carries files to people, here those
that the failed tests wrote, and to later jobs, which get them with
`actions/download-artifact`; its name must be unique within the run, hence the
version and the system in it. `actions/checkout` fetches only the commit
itself, without the history or the tags, so `git describe`, and tools that take
the version of a package from its tags, such as setuptools-scm, need
`fetch-depth: 0`.

setup-uv caches the packages it downloads by itself. For other tools,
`actions/cache` saves a directory under a key, such as
`key: deps-${{ hashFiles('requirements.txt') }}`, which changes with the file.


## Release a version {#sec-tag-release}

```yaml
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]

permissions:
  contents: write  # to create the release

jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - run: gh release create "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" --verify-tag --generate-notes
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          GH_REPO: ${{ github.repository }}
```

Pushing the tag of a version ([](git.qmd#sec-tag)) makes a release of it on
GitHub. The job needs no checkout, since `gh` acts on the repository that
`GH_REPO` names. The notes that GitHub generates list the pull requests merged
since the last release; they do not replace the changelog, which says what
changed for users ([](../../principles/documenting.qmd#sec-changelog)). Files
named after the tag, such as `dist/*`, are attached to the release, from a job
that built them or downloaded them as an artifact (@sec-passing). A package
index such as PyPI accepts a package without a stored token through trusted
publishing, which lets a job with `id-token: write` prove that it runs in this
repository.


## Follow and debug runs {#sec-debug}

```bash
gh run list --workflow tests.yml   # the latest runs of a workflow
gh run watch                       # follow a run until it ends
gh run view <run> --log-failed     # the log of the steps that failed
gh run rerun <run> --failed --debug  # run the failed jobs again, verbose
gh run download <run> -n figures   # an artifact of a run
gh workflow run tests.yml --ref fix-units  # start a run by hand
actionlint                         # check the workflow files
```

actionlint checks workflow files before they are pushed: their syntax, their
expressions, the inputs of common actions, and values that someone else
controls used in a script (@sec-shell). Most mistakes that would otherwise show
up only as a failed run, minutes later, show up there. No tool runs a workflow
on your own machine exactly as GitHub does, although act comes close, with
containers that resemble the runners. Keep the commands of a job in a script or
a Makefile that the workflow calls, so that they can be run and debugged
anywhere; this site's own workflow does no more than `make site`.


## Keep the actions current {#sec-dependabot}

```yaml
# .github/dependabot.yml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: github-actions
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: monthly
```

Dependabot opens a pull request when an action has a new version, for actions
named by a tag and by a hash alike, and so keeps them current without moving
them silently (@sec-permissions).
